topics.title: Volatility 3 Command Syntax and Usage
topics.content: Volatility 3 is a complete rewrite of the Volatility memory forensics framework, designed for Python 3 with improved performance and modularity. The basic command structure is: vol -f <memory_dump> <plugin>. Unlike Volatility 2, you no longer need to specify a profile - Volatility 3 uses symbol tables (ISF files) and autodetects the operating system. The framework supports multiple memory formats including raw dumps, crash dumps, hibernation files, VMware snapshots (.vmem), VirtualBox core dumps, and LiME format for Linux. Key flags include: -f for specifying the memory file, -o for output directory, -r for renderer selection (quick, json, csv, pretty), --single-location for specific offset analysis, and -v for verbose output. Volatility 3 plugins are namespaced by OS: windows.*, linux.*, and mac.*. You can list all available plugins with 'vol --help' or 'vol -f dump.mem windows. --help' for Windows-specific plugins. The framework automatically downloads required symbol tables from the Volatility symbol server, though you can specify custom symbol paths with --symbol-dirs. For large memory dumps (16GB+), consider using the --cache option to speed up repeated analysis. Output can be redirected to files using standard shell redirection or the built-in renderers for JSON/CSV export.

topics.title: Memory Acquisition Methods
topics.content: Before using Volatility, you need a memory image. Memory acquisition is the process of capturing the contents of RAM while preserving volatile evidence. For Windows, popular tools include: WinPmem (open-source, supports multiple output formats), FTK Imager (AccessData, GUI-based, widely accepted in court), DumpIt (single executable, no installation), Belkasoft RAM Capturer (free, portable), and Magnet RAM Capture. For Linux, LiME (Linux Memory Extractor) is the standard, compiled as a kernel module that dumps memory to file or network. For macOS, osxpmem or MacQuisition are used. Memory formats supported by Volatility 3 include: raw/dd format (simple memory dump), Microsoft crash dumps (.dmp), hibernation files (hiberfil.sys), VMware snapshots (.vmem), VirtualBox core dumps, QEMU memory dumps, and LiME format (.lime). When acquiring memory, time is critical - RAM is volatile and changes constantly. Minimize interaction with the target system, use trusted acquisition tools from a USB drive, and document the acquisition process including timestamps, hash values, and chain of custody. For live forensics, consider that the acquisition tool itself will appear in memory. Remote acquisition is possible using tools like F-Response or Velociraptor.

topics.title: Symbol Tables and ISF Files
topics.content: Volatility 3 uses Intermediate Symbol Format (ISF) files instead of the profile system from Volatility 2. ISF files are JSON representations of operating system debugging symbols that tell Volatility the memory layout of kernel structures like EPROCESS, KTHREAD, and other critical data structures. For Windows analysis, Volatility downloads PDB files from the Microsoft Symbol Server and converts them to ISF format. The symbols are stored in a local cache (typically ~/.volatility3/symbols or %USERPROFILE%/.volatility3/symbols on Windows). For Linux and macOS, you may need to generate custom symbols using the dwarf2json tool against a kernel with debugging symbols. The symbol files are critical - without correct symbols, Volatility cannot parse memory structures and plugins will fail or return incorrect data. Common issues include: symbol download failures (firewall/proxy blocks), mismatched symbols (wrong OS version), and missing symbols for custom/patched kernels. You can specify additional symbol directories with --symbol-dirs and use --offline to prevent network symbol downloads. For enterprise environments, consider hosting an internal symbol mirror.

topics.title: Process Enumeration with pslist, pstree, psscan
topics.content: Process enumeration is fundamental to memory forensics. Volatility 3 provides three complementary plugins for process discovery. PsList walks the ActiveProcessLinks doubly-linked list in EPROCESS structures - this is how the OS tracks running processes. PsTree presents processes hierarchically showing parent-child relationships, essential for understanding process spawning patterns. PsScan uses pool tag scanning to find EPROCESS structures in memory, including terminated and unlinked (hidden) processes. The key insight: rootkits often use Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) to unlink processes from the ActiveProcessLinks list while keeping them running. Such hidden processes appear in PsScan but not PsList. Comparing outputs reveals hidden malware. When analyzing output, examine: suspicious process names (misspellings like 'svch0st.exe'), unusual parent-child relationships (cmd.exe spawning from explorer.exe is normal, from services.exe is suspicious), processes with no parent (orphaned), processes in unusual sessions, single-threaded svchost.exe (normally multi-threaded), and processes with abnormal handle counts. Timestamp analysis reveals timeline - processes started at system boot vs. during user session vs. at unusual hours.

topics.title: Command Line Analysis with cmdline
topics.content: The cmdline plugin extracts command line arguments for each process, revealing how processes were launched and with what parameters. This is critical for malware analysis as attackers often pass encoded commands, download URLs, or configuration parameters via command line. The plugin reads the PEB (Process Environment Block) structure to extract the full command line string. Key things to look for: encoded PowerShell commands (base64 -enc, -e, -EncodedCommand), curl/wget downloading malware, unusual script interpreters (wscript, cscript, mshta), processes launched from temp directories, regsvr32/rundll32 with remote URLs (Living off the Land), net/sc/schtasks for persistence, and any obfuscated or unusually long command lines. Process Hollowing and injection attacks may show legitimate process names but with suspicious command lines. Compare command lines against known-good baselines - svchost.exe should always have a -k parameter, for example. Empty or very short command lines for complex processes may indicate manual patching or evasion.

topics.title: DLL Analysis with dlllist and ldrmodules
topics.content: DLL analysis reveals what libraries a process has loaded, essential for detecting DLL injection and malicious module loading. The dlllist plugin walks the PEB InLoadOrderModuleList to show DLLs a process believes it has loaded. It displays base address, size, and full path for each DLL. Key analysis points: DLLs loaded from unusual paths (temp, appdata, downloads), missing legitimate system DLLs, DLLs with suspicious names or version info, and DLLs loaded but not in expected process. DLL injection techniques include LoadLibrary injection (DLL appears in lists), reflective DLL injection (DLL may not appear in standard lists), and DLL hollowing (legitimate DLL path but malicious code). For deeper analysis, use handles plugin to find open handles to DLL files, and malfind to detect injected code that may not appear as proper DLLs. Compare DLL lists between similar processes - all svchost.exe instances should have similar base DLLs loaded. Size anomalies may indicate patching or hollowing.

topics.title: Handle Analysis
topics.content: The handles plugin reveals kernel objects each process has open, including files, registry keys, mutexes, events, threads, and other processes. This is powerful for understanding process behavior and relationships. Handle analysis reveals: files being accessed or locked, registry keys being monitored or modified, inter-process communication via shared objects, mutexes used for single-instance enforcement (malware often creates unique mutexes), and process injection indicators (handles to other processes). Malware analysis: check for handles to sensitive files (SAM, SYSTEM hives), handles to lsass.exe from non-security processes, suspicious mutex names, and handles to remote process memory. Network-related handles may indicate network activity not visible in netscan. The output can be filtered by object type (File, Key, Process, Thread, Mutant, Event) to focus analysis. Large numbers of handles to system processes from user-mode applications may indicate malicious activity.

topics.title: Network Connection Analysis with netscan
topics.content: The netscan plugin extracts network connection information from memory, revealing active TCP connections, UDP endpoints, and listening sockets. Unlike live netstat which shows current connections, memory forensics captures point-in-time state that may include terminated connections still in memory. The output shows: local address and port, remote address and port (for TCP), connection state (ESTABLISHED, LISTENING, CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT, etc.), and owning process PID. This is critical for identifying command-and-control (C2) communications, data exfiltration, and lateral movement. Key analysis points: connections to external IPs from suspicious processes, high-numbered ephemeral ports (common for C2), connections from processes that shouldn't have network activity (notepad.exe, calc.exe), multiple connections to same IP from different processes, and connections to known-bad IPs (check against threat intelligence). UDP endpoints are particularly interesting as they may indicate DNS exfiltration or UDP-based C2. LISTENING ports reveal services that were available for exploitation. Compare netscan output with expected network behavior for the system role.

topics.title: Identifying Command and Control Communications
topics.content: Command and Control (C2) detection is a primary goal of memory forensics. Malware needs to communicate with attackers, and network artifacts in memory can reveal these channels. Key indicators: connections from unusual processes (notepad.exe, calc.exe, explorer.exe with external connections), connections to external IPs on suspicious ports (4444, 5555, 8080, 9999 are common C2 ports), multiple processes connecting to same external IP, beaconing patterns (regular interval connections), connections to IP addresses instead of domains, DNS over HTTPS artifacts, and connections to cloud services commonly abused (pastebin, discord, telegram). Combine netscan with process analysis: if PowerShell connects to an external IP, check cmdline for encoded commands. Correlate with timeline - C2 often established shortly after initial compromise. Check for proxy-aware malware by looking for connections to internal proxy servers. Some advanced malware uses DNS tunneling (look for DNS activity from non-system processes) or ICMP channels (harder to detect in memory). Cross-reference IPs with threat intelligence feeds for known-bad infrastructure.

topics.title: Detecting Code Injection with Malfind
topics.content: The malfind plugin is one of the most powerful tools for detecting code injection in memory. It identifies memory regions with suspicious characteristics, specifically looking for executable memory (PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE or PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY) that is not backed by a file on disk. Legitimate code comes from DLLs and executables mapped from files - injected code typically exists only in memory. Malfind examines each process's VAD (Virtual Address Descriptor) tree and flags regions that: have execute permissions AND write permissions (RWX), are committed memory not backed by files, and contain content that may be executable code. The output includes a hexdump and disassembly of suspicious regions. Key indicators: MZ headers (PE files injected into memory), shellcode patterns (NOP sleds, syscall stubs), strings referencing system calls or network activity. False positives occur with JIT compilers (.NET CLR, JavaScript engines), packed executables that unpack in memory, and some security products. However, these should be investigated to confirm legitimacy. Combine malfind with process analysis - injected code in a legitimate process (svchost, explorer) is more suspicious than in a specialized application.

topics.title: VAD Analysis for Memory Forensics
topics.content: VAD (Virtual Address Descriptor) trees describe the virtual memory layout of each process. Understanding VADs is crucial for advanced memory forensics as they reveal all memory regions, their protections, backing files, and relationships. The vadinfo plugin provides detailed information about each VAD including start/end addresses, memory protection flags, whether the region is private or mapped, and the backing file path if applicable. VAD analysis reveals: memory regions with suspicious protections, unbacked executable regions (injected code), memory-mapped files, heap regions, stack locations, and PEB/TEB structures. The vadwalk plugin shows the VAD tree structure itself. Key protection flags to watch: PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (RWX - rarely legitimate), PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY (often used in process hollowing), and changes from initial protections. Memory regions can transition through protection changes - malware often allocates RW, writes code, then changes to RX. VAD analysis combined with malfind provides comprehensive code injection detection.

topics.title: YARA Scanning in Memory
topics.content: YARA scanning allows you to search memory for specific patterns, strings, or signatures. The yarascan plugin in Volatility 3 applies YARA rules against process memory or kernel memory. This is powerful for: detecting known malware families, finding specific strings or patterns, identifying malware variants, and custom IOC hunting. YARA rules can match on strings, hex patterns, regular expressions, file magic, and conditions combining multiple patterns. You can scan specific processes with --pid, kernel memory with --kernel, or all processes. The output shows which rules matched, in which process, and at what address. Writing effective YARA rules requires understanding malware behavior - look for unique strings, API call patterns, encryption constants, or C2 communication markers. Pre-built YARA rule sets are available from security researchers and organizations. For memory forensics, consider rules that detect injected code patterns, shellcode signatures, and known APT tools.

topics.title: File Scanning with filescan
topics.content: The filescan plugin scans memory for FILE_OBJECT structures, revealing files that were open at the time of memory capture. This includes files that may have been deleted from disk but remain referenced in memory, providing recovery opportunities for critical evidence. The output shows the kernel object offset, file path, and associated information. Key analysis points: look for suspicious files in temp directories, files with unusual extensions, files associated with malicious processes, deleted files still in memory, and files being accessed at unusual times. File paths reveal malware locations, data staging directories, and dropped tools. Combine with dumpfiles to extract file contents when available. For malware analysis, look for: executables in user directories, scripts in temp folders, files with double extensions (.pdf.exe), and files matching known malware naming conventions. Files in Windows\Temp, Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp, and Users\*\Downloads are high-priority for investigation.

topics.title: Extracting Files with dumpfiles
topics.content: The dumpfiles plugin extracts file contents from memory, enabling recovery of files that may be deleted from disk, encrypted by ransomware, or otherwise inaccessible. Files in memory exist as memory sections - DataSectionObject for file data and ImageSectionObject for executable images. The plugin can extract files by process (--pid), by physical offset (--physaddr), or by virtual address. Extracted files may be complete or partial depending on whether all pages were in memory at capture time. This is invaluable for recovering: malware executables before they were deleted, exfiltrated documents, encryption keys, and configuration files. For best results, specify the output directory with -o. The plugin attempts to recover the original filename but may fall back to offset-based naming. Extracted executables can be submitted to sandbox analysis or reverse engineered. Extracted documents may contain sensitive data relevant to data breach investigations.

topics.title: Registry Hive Enumeration
topics.content: Windows Registry hives contain critical system and user configuration data, and their in-memory representation often contains evidence of malicious activity. The hivelist plugin shows all registry hives loaded in memory with their virtual addresses and file paths. Key hives include: SAM (local accounts and passwords), SECURITY (security policies and LSA secrets), SYSTEM (system configuration, services, drivers), SOFTWARE (installed software and settings), NTUSER.DAT (per-user settings), and UsrClass.dat (user shell settings). Registry analysis reveals: persistence mechanisms (Run keys, Services), malware configuration, user activity traces, recently accessed files, USB device history, and system modifications. The hivescan plugin uses pool scanning to find hives that may be unlinked (hidden by rootkits). Compare hivelist and hivescan results - discrepancies may indicate registry hiding. Each hive is identified by its file path and virtual address, which is needed for printkey operations.

topics.title: Registry Key Extraction with printkey
topics.content: The printkey plugin extracts specific registry keys and values from memory, essential for finding persistence mechanisms, system configuration, and evidence of compromise. You specify the hive offset (from hivelist) and the key path. Common investigation targets: Run/RunOnce keys (HKLM and HKCU) for autostart persistence, Services key for malicious services, CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options for debugger hijacking, Winlogon keys for shell replacement, AppInit_DLLs for DLL injection, and Explorer\Shell Folders for startup folder locations. The output shows key last write time, subkeys, and values with their data. Analyze timestamps to correlate with incident timeline - recently modified keys during attack window are high-priority. Check for obfuscated or encoded values, unusual executable paths, and keys referencing temp directories.

topics.title: UserAssist Analysis for Execution History
topics.content: The UserAssist registry keys record program execution history for each user, providing valuable forensic evidence of what programs were run. The data is stored ROT13-encoded in NTUSER.DAT under Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist. The userassist plugin decodes this automatically, showing: program path, run count, last execution time, and focus time (how long the application was in foreground). This is crucial for establishing: what the attacker executed, when they ran specific tools, which malware was manually launched, and user activity patterns. Note that UserAssist only tracks GUI applications launched through Explorer - command-line tools and services are not recorded. Recent execution indicates the program was run close to memory capture time. High run counts suggest repeated use. Focus time helps distinguish briefly launched programs from those actively used.

topics.title: Service Enumeration with svcscan
topics.content: The svcscan plugin enumerates Windows services from memory, revealing both running and stopped services. Services are a common persistence mechanism for malware as they run with SYSTEM privileges and start automatically. The plugin reads service information from the Service Control Manager (SCM) database in memory. Key fields include: service name, display name, binary path, service type (kernel driver, user mode, shared process), start type (auto, manual, disabled), service state, and PID if running. Look for: services with unusual names or display names, services running from temp or user directories, services with suspicious binary paths, disabled security services, and newly created services matching incident timeline. Legitimate services typically run from System32, Program Files, or established vendor directories. Services in temp directories, AppData, or Downloads are highly suspicious. Compare against known-good service baseline for the system.

topics.title: Driver Analysis with driverscan and modules
topics.content: Driver analysis is critical for detecting kernel-mode rootkits and malicious drivers. The driverscan plugin scans for DRIVER_OBJECT structures in memory pool, while modules lists loaded kernel modules from the module list. Comparing results reveals hidden drivers - those in driverscan but not in modules may be unlinked (rootkit technique). Key analysis points: unsigned drivers (legitimate drivers should be signed on modern Windows), drivers loaded from unusual paths, drivers with suspicious names, drivers not matching known-good baseline, and recently loaded drivers during attack window. Malicious drivers can: hide processes and files, intercept system calls, log keystrokes, provide persistent backdoors, and modify kernel behavior. Driver signing enforcement can be bypassed through vulnerable signed drivers, test signing mode, or exploiting vulnerabilities. Cross-reference driver files with filescan and attempt extraction with dumpfiles for analysis.

topics.title: Mutex Analysis for Malware Identification
topics.content: Mutexes (mutants) are synchronization objects often used by malware to prevent multiple instances from running simultaneously. Each malware family typically uses unique mutex names, making them valuable for identification and threat intelligence. The mutantscan plugin scans for KMUTANT structures in memory pool. Malware mutexes often have: unique or random-looking names, names containing campaign identifiers, base64-like strings, and names referencing the malware family. Famous examples include 'DCRat-Mutex' for DCRat, various GUIDs for specific campaigns, and custom strings like 'Global\\[malwarename]'. Compare discovered mutexes against threat intelligence databases - matching mutex names can identify the malware family immediately. Legitimate mutexes typically have descriptive names related to application functionality. Unusual mutex names, especially in combination with suspicious processes, warrant investigation.

topics.title: Password Hash Extraction with hashdump
topics.content: The hashdump plugin extracts Windows password hashes from the SAM (Security Accounts Manager) database in memory. This provides the same information as the SAM file but directly from memory, which may include accounts not on disk (domain cached credentials). The output includes: username, RID (Relative Identifier), LM hash (legacy, often empty on modern Windows), and NTLM hash. These hashes can be cracked offline using tools like Hashcat or John the Ripper, or used directly in Pass-the-Hash attacks. Important context: hashdump shows LOCAL accounts only. For domain accounts, use lsadump or mimikatz artifacts. Empty LM hash (aad3b435b51404ee) indicates LM hashing is disabled (good security). The NTLM hash is the primary target for cracking or PTH. From a forensics perspective, hashdump reveals: what local accounts exist, potential weak passwords after cracking, and evidence of compromised accounts if you find unexpected accounts.

topics.title: LSA Secrets Extraction with lsadump
topics.content: The lsadump plugin extracts LSA (Local Security Authority) secrets from memory. LSA secrets include: service account passwords (for services running as specific accounts), auto-logon passwords (DefaultPassword), cached domain credentials, DPAPI master keys, and other sensitive security data. This provides attackers with additional credentials beyond the SAM database. DefaultPassword is particularly concerning as it enables auto-logon and exposes plaintext passwords. Service passwords reveal credentials that may be reused across the network. $MACHINE.ACC is the machine account password for domain-joined computers. Extracting these secrets from memory gives the same results as running mimikatz sekurlsa::lsadump but through pure memory forensics. From an IR perspective, check for: unexpected services with stored passwords, auto-logon configured on servers, and credential exposure.

topics.title: Detecting Mimikatz and Credential Theft Tools
topics.content: Mimikatz and similar credential theft tools leave artifacts in memory that can be detected through forensic analysis. Detection approaches include: finding mimikatz process (may be renamed), detecting access to lsass.exe from unusual processes, finding mimikatz strings in memory, identifying mimikatz module patterns, and detecting the results of credential dumping (plaintext passwords in memory). Key indicators: handles to lsass.exe from non-security processes, RWX memory in lsass containing credential data, specific Mimikatz strings like 'sekurlsa', 'logonpasswords', 'wdigest', and presence of credential structures outside normal lsass memory. YARA rules for Mimikatz signatures are highly effective. Also check for: procdump.exe usage (lsass dumping), comsvcs.dll!MiniDump abuse, and direct lsass memory reading attempts. The presence of any credential theft tool indicates serious compromise requiring immediate response.

topics.title: SSDT Hooking Detection
topics.content: The SSDT (System Service Descriptor Table) contains pointers to kernel functions that handle system calls. Rootkits can modify these pointers to redirect system calls to their own malicious handlers, enabling process hiding, file hiding, and other stealth techniques. The ssdt plugin in Volatility displays the SSDT entries and identifies hooks by checking if function pointers point outside the expected kernel module (ntoskrnl.exe). A hooked entry will show a function address in a different module - often the rootkit driver. Key analysis: compare function addresses against expected ntoskrnl range, identify which syscalls are hooked (NtQuerySystemInformation for process hiding, NtQueryDirectoryFile for file hiding), and correlate with suspicious drivers. Modern Windows (x64 with PatchGuard) makes SSDT hooking harder but not impossible - rootkits may use other techniques or disable PatchGuard. Historical SSDT hooking is still relevant for older systems and some advanced rootkits.

topics.title: Callback and Notification Detection
topics.content: Windows provides legitimate kernel callback mechanisms that rootkits abuse for persistence and monitoring. The callbacks plugin enumerates registered callback routines including: PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine (process creation/termination), PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine (thread creation), PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine (image/DLL loading), CmRegisterCallback (registry operations), ObRegisterCallbacks (object manager), and filesystem filter callbacks. Rootkits register malicious callbacks to: monitor all process creation, log all registry access, intercept file operations, hide malicious activity, and maintain persistence. Legitimate callbacks come from security software, Windows itself, and system drivers. Suspicious callbacks: those registered by unsigned drivers, drivers from unusual paths, or drivers matching known malware. Cross-reference callback owners with driver analysis to identify malicious registrations.

topics.title: Detecting Hidden Processes and DKOM
topics.content: Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) is a rootkit technique that manipulates kernel data structures to hide processes, drivers, and other objects. For process hiding, rootkits unlink the EPROCESS structure from the ActiveProcessLinks list while keeping the process running. Detection relies on cross-validation: compare pslist (walks linked list) with psscan (scans memory pools). Processes in psscan but not pslist are hidden. Other DKOM techniques include: driver unlinking (modscan vs modules), handle table manipulation, and object header corruption. Detection methodology: run multiple enumeration plugins that use different detection methods, compare outputs, and investigate discrepancies. Note that terminated processes also appear in psscan but not pslist - check ExitTime to differentiate. DKOM detection is a core memory forensics skill for identifying advanced threats.

topics.title: Timeline Analysis with timeliner
topics.content: Timeline analysis correlates events across multiple data sources to reconstruct the sequence of attacker activity. The timeliner plugin in Volatility 3 extracts timestamped events from various sources: process creation/exit times, network connection times, file access times, registry key modifications, and more. The output is typically formatted for import into timeline analysis tools like log2timeline/plaso, Timeline Explorer, or custom analysis. Key benefits: establishing attack timeline, correlating seemingly unrelated events, identifying initial compromise time, and understanding attack progression. Analysis approach: identify earliest malicious artifact, work backward to find initial access, work forward to map full impact. Timestamps in memory are point-in-time captures - they show state at dump time plus historical timestamps for events. Correlate with filesystem MFT, event logs, and network logs for comprehensive timeline. Look for clustering of suspicious events - attackers often perform multiple actions in short windows.

topics.title: String Analysis in Memory
topics.content: String analysis extracts readable text from memory to find artifacts, commands, URLs, credentials, and other evidence. While Volatility provides structured analysis, raw string searching catches artifacts that structured plugins miss. The strings plugin in Volatility associates discovered strings with their memory locations and owning processes. Key targets: URLs and IP addresses, file paths, command lines, credentials (passwords, API keys), malware configuration, encryption keys, and attacker commands. Combine with standard 'strings' command-line tool for comprehensive extraction, then grep for specific patterns. For process-specific strings, dump process memory first then run strings. Regular expressions enhance searching: IP patterns, URL patterns, base64 patterns, etc. Unicode strings (wide strings) are common in Windows - use both ASCII and Unicode extraction. Large memory dumps generate millions of strings - targeted searching is essential.

topics.title: Memory Carving and Raw Analysis
topics.content: Memory carving extracts embedded files and data structures from raw memory without relying on filesystem metadata. Techniques include: file header/footer carving (finding MZ for PE files, PK for ZIP), structure carving (finding specific data structures by signature), and pattern-based carving (finding data matching known formats). Tools: foremost, scalpel, binwalk can carve memory dumps directly. Key targets: embedded executables (malware dropped in memory), documents, images, encryption keys, and network packets. Carving is valuable when: structured plugins fail, you need to recover specific file types, or you're searching for artifacts outside process memory. Process: identify target format signatures, scan raw memory for matches, extract and analyze candidates. Memory is less structured than disk - expect more false positives. Combine with Volatility analysis to focus carving on specific memory regions.

topics.title: Linux Process Analysis
topics.content: Linux memory forensics in Volatility 3 uses the linux.* plugin namespace. Linux process analysis examines task_struct structures in kernel memory. Key plugins: linux.pslist.PsList (walks task list), linux.pstree.PsTree (hierarchical view), linux.psaux.PsAux (ps aux equivalent with command lines). Unlike Windows, Linux process hiding requires different techniques - look for kernel module-based hiding, LD_PRELOAD hooks, and process namespace manipulation. Linux-specific indicators: processes running as root that shouldn't be, unusual init-spawned processes, processes with suspicious command lines, hidden processes via rootkit, and container/namespace escape attempts. Memory acquisition on Linux typically uses LiME (Linux Memory Extractor), and symbol generation requires the exact kernel version with debug symbols (dwarf2json). Cross-reference process analysis with network connections (linux.sockstat) and file descriptors.

topics.title: Linux Network Analysis
topics.content: Linux network forensics uses linux.sockstat to enumerate network connections from memory. The plugin reads socket structures from kernel memory, providing information similar to 'netstat' but from the memory dump. Output includes: protocol (TCP/UDP), local address and port, remote address and port, socket state, and owning process. Unlike Windows netscan, Linux socket analysis may show Unix domain sockets and raw sockets in addition to TCP/UDP. Key indicators: connections to external IPs from non-network processes, reverse shells (high port to external IP), connections on unusual ports, and sockets owned by suspicious processes. Linux servers often have legitimate network services - compare against expected services for the server role. Look for connections from web shells (apache/nginx child processes with external connections), SSH tunnels, and data exfiltration channels.

topics.title: Linux Rootkit Detection
topics.content: Linux kernel rootkits typically load as Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) that hook system calls, hide processes, and modify kernel behavior. Detection techniques: linux.lsmod (list loaded modules), linux.check_syscall (detect syscall table hooks), linux.hidden_modules (find hidden modules), and linux.keyboard_notifiers (keylogger detection). LKM rootkits hide by: unlinking from module list (compare lsmod vs module scan), hooking system calls (check_syscall detects), and using kallsyms manipulation. Common hooked syscalls: sys_read (hide network traffic), sys_getdents (hide files), sys_open (hide files), and sys_kill (protect processes). Also check: /proc manipulation, netfilter hooks, and function pointer hijacking. Modern rootkits may use eBPF for stealthy hooking. Cross-reference process visibility between multiple methods, similar to Windows DKOM detection.

topics.title: macOS Process Analysis
topics.content: macOS (Darwin/XNU kernel) memory forensics uses the mac.* plugin namespace in Volatility 3. macOS process analysis examines proc structures in kernel memory, similar to Linux task_struct. Key plugins: mac.pslist.PsList (process enumeration), mac.pstree.PsTree (hierarchical view), and mac.psaux.PsAux (with command lines). macOS-specific considerations: System Integrity Protection (SIP) may limit rootkit activity, kernel extensions (kexts) are the macOS equivalent of LKMs, and modern macOS uses APFS with encryption. Suspicious indicators: processes spawned from /tmp or user directories, LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons for persistence, unusual child processes of system processes, and processes with suspicious bundle identifiers. macOS Gatekeeper and notarization provide some protection, but attackers bypass with unsigned code or social engineering. Memory acquisition on macOS uses osxpmem or commercial tools.

topics.title: macOS Network and Persistence Analysis
topics.content: macOS network analysis uses mac.netstat (or similar plugins) to enumerate network connections from memory. Key differences from other platforms: macOS uses a unique implementation of the BSD socket API, kernel extensions (kexts) can intercept network traffic, and network extensions framework provides modern filtering. For persistence detection: LaunchAgents (/Library/LaunchAgents, ~/Library/LaunchAgents) run as user, LaunchDaemons (/Library/LaunchDaemons) run as root, Login Items, and kernel extensions. Use mac.lsmod to list loaded kernel extensions - malicious kexts are rare but powerful rootkits. Check for: unusual kexts not from Apple or known vendors, network connections from unexpected processes, persistence in LaunchAgent plists, and cron jobs. macOS Catalina and later restrict kext loading, making user-land persistence more common in modern attacks.

topics.title: Symbol Table Issues and Resolution
topics.content: Symbol table issues are the most common Volatility 3 problems. Symptoms include: 'Unsupported operating system', 'No suitable symbol table found', 'Unable to find a valid DOS header', and plugins returning no results or errors. Root causes: missing symbol files, corrupted downloads, network issues preventing symbol download, unsupported OS versions, and corrupted memory dumps. Resolution steps: 1) Run with -vv to see symbol loading details, 2) Check if symbols are cached in ~/.volatility3/symbols, 3) Manually download PDB from Microsoft Symbol Server, 4) Use dwarf2json for Linux/macOS symbols, 5) Verify memory dump with windows.info or equivalent. For air-gapped environments, pre-download symbols for target OS versions. Symbol mismatches cause subtle errors - plugins may run but return incorrect data. Always verify windows.info output matches expected OS before trusting other plugin output.

topics.title: Memory Dump Format and Corruption Issues
topics.content: Memory dump format issues prevent Volatility from parsing the memory correctly. Common problems: wrong file format, corrupted acquisition, incomplete dump, unsupported virtualization format, and hibernation file issues. Volatility 3 supports: raw memory (dd-style), Microsoft crash dump (.dmp), hibernation files (hiberfil.sys - requires decompression for Win8+), VMware snapshots (.vmem), VirtualBox memory dumps, LiME format (.lime), and EWF/E01 (with libewf). Diagnosis: use 'file' command to identify format, check file size matches expected RAM size, verify with hex editor for valid headers. Raw dumps should show valid kernel structures; crash dumps have specific headers. For VMware, ensure you have the .vmem file not just .vmss (snapshot state). Partial or truncated dumps may still be partially analyzable - Volatility will report gaps. Hibernation files from Windows 8+ are compressed and require extraction.

topics.title: Performance Optimization
topics.content: Memory analysis can be slow, especially for large dumps (16GB+). Optimization strategies: use --cache-path for repeated analysis (avoids reprocessing), filter plugins with --pid when possible, use faster storage (SSD vs HDD), increase available RAM for processing, run specific plugins rather than comprehensive scans, use renderers that don't require formatting (quick vs pretty), and parallelize independent plugins. Volatility 3 is more efficient than Volatility 2 but still resource-intensive. For very large dumps (64GB+), consider: splitting analysis across multiple sessions, focusing on specific processes of interest, using grep/string analysis before structured plugins, and running on workstations with 32GB+ RAM. psscan is particularly slow (full memory scan); use pslist first, psscan only when looking for hidden processes. Disable unused automagic features if you know the memory format.

topics.title: Common Plugin Errors and Fixes
topics.content: Plugin errors range from informative warnings to complete failures. Common issues and solutions: 'Unsupported operating system' - symbol mismatch, run windows.info first; 'Required memory is not valid' - memory region paged out, normal for some entries; 'No suitable layer found' - wrong memory format or corrupted dump; 'AttributeError' - symbol version mismatch; 'Unable to find symbol' - symbols don't match OS version; empty results - may be normal (no network connections) or error (symbols wrong). Debug approach: 1) Run with -vv for verbose output, 2) Try windows.info first to verify basic functionality, 3) Check symbol loading succeeded, 4) Verify dump format with file/xxd, 5) Try on known-good test dump. Some plugins are OS-version specific; check plugin documentation. Report bugs with full verbose output, memory dump hash, and OS version.

topics.title: Ransomware Investigation Workflow
topics.content: Ransomware memory forensics can recover encryption keys, identify the ransomware family, and understand encryption scope before keys are lost. Critical first step: capture memory IMMEDIATELY before reboot or shutdown - keys are in RAM. Workflow: 1) Acquire memory with minimal system interaction, 2) Run process analysis to find ransomware process, 3) Extract process memory for key recovery, 4) Search strings for encryption keys, wallet addresses, C2 URLs, 5) Identify ransomware family via YARA, mutex names, strings, 6) Timeline analysis to understand encryption scope, 7) Network analysis for C2 and data exfiltration. Key recovery: many ransomware families keep encryption keys in process memory during operation. Tools like ransomware-specific decryptors can use dumped process memory. Look for: large random-looking hex strings (potential keys), RSA public keys, ransom note templates, Bitcoin/Monero addresses, and file extension modifications. Document findings for law enforcement and recovery efforts.

topics.title: APT/Advanced Threat Investigation Workflow
topics.content: APT investigations require comprehensive analysis as attackers use sophisticated techniques to evade detection. Workflow: 1) Initial triage - process, network, malfind for quick wins, 2) Cross-reference pslist vs psscan for hidden processes, 3) Analyze all network connections for C2 infrastructure, 4) Check for code injection and fileless malware, 5) Registry persistence analysis, 6) Credential theft indicators (lsass access, mimikatz signatures), 7) Timeline analysis for attack progression, 8) YARA scanning with APT-specific rules. APT indicators: sophisticated C2 (domain fronting, DNS tunneling), memory-only implants, extensive lateral movement, credential theft, and data staging. Look for: abnormal process relationships, encoded PowerShell, living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins), timestomping evidence, and connections to known APT infrastructure. Document everything for threat intelligence sharing and attribution efforts.

topics.title: Insider Threat and Data Exfiltration Investigation
topics.content: Insider threat investigations focus on authorized users misusing access to steal data. Memory forensics reveals: files accessed and potentially copied, USB device connections, cloud upload activity, email attachments, and encryption of sensitive data for exfiltration. Workflow: 1) Process analysis for file access tools (7zip, WinRAR, cloud clients), 2) Handle analysis for accessed sensitive files, 3) Network analysis for cloud uploads and unusual destinations, 4) String analysis for file paths and credentials, 5) Registry for USB device history and recent files, 6) Timeline analysis correlating user logon with suspicious activity. Key artifacts: clipboard contents, document paths in process memory, cloud sync client activity, and staging directories. Unlike external attacks, insiders have legitimate access - focus on policy violations and unusual volume/patterns of access.

topics.title: Incident Response Triage Workflow
topics.content: Effective incident response requires rapid initial triage to determine scope and severity. The standard memory triage workflow provides quick wins before deep analysis. Workflow order: 1) windows.info - verify dump validity and OS version, 2) windows.pslist - quick process overview, 3) windows.pstree - understand process relationships, 4) windows.netscan - identify network connections and potential C2, 5) windows.malfind - find code injection quickly, 6) windows.cmdline - see executed commands, 7) windows.svcscan - check for malicious services. This sequence takes 10-15 minutes and provides immediate answers about compromise indicators. Based on initial findings, prioritize deeper analysis: hidden processes require psscan, network IOCs require correlation with threat intelligence, code injection requires extraction and analysis, and credential theft indicators require hashdump/lsadump. Document initial findings for stakeholder briefing and guide subsequent response actions.
